speaker: Kathleen Sullivan
title: Supreme Court and Appellate Advocacy | Kathleen Sullivan
question: In appellate courts, what is the practical tradeoff between strict fixed oral argument time limits and flexible judge-directed extensions?
guest: Sometimes not every argument needs to fit into an hour. Sometimes an argument is really finished before then, and sometimes an argument may benefit from a little more. So I suppose I would like it if sometimes we could go past thirty minutes a side the way sometimes in the circuits you can go past your allotted time if the questioning warrants it. That would be the only thing. I recognize that would create a lot of discretion and potentially a sense of inequality among cases, but there have just been some times when I thought the questioning could have gone longer.

points.core: Fixed oral argument time caps mismatch how long different cases actually need.
points.note: Accept: uniform allotments (such as 30 minutes per side) leaving some arguments finished early while cutting off complex cases prematurely. Do not credit: generic remarks that courts have busy dockets.

points.core: Allowing arguments to run overtime lets judges finish productive lines of questioning.
points.note: Accept: flexible extensions (as in federal circuits or extended questioning rounds) when bench questioning genuinely warrants deeper exploration. Do not credit: advocating unlimited speech time for lawyers.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The tradeoff is essentially predictability and equality versus thoroughness and responsiveness.

Strict fixed limits keep dockets moving, let courts schedule several cases per sitting, and treat every litigant alike: each side gets the same time regardless of the judges' interest or the advocate's reputation. They also force counsel to prioritize their strongest points. The cost is that argument can end just as the court reaches the hardest question, and heavy questioning from the bench can consume an advocate's time, leaving key issues or rebuttal unaddressed.

Flexible, judge-directed extensions let the court pursue what actually troubles it, give complex cases the time they need, and ensure every judge gets questions answered. The US Supreme Court's post-2020 format, with seriatim questioning after the timed period, illustrates this; arguments now often run well past the nominal hour. The costs are longer and less predictable sessions, difficulty for counsel in pacing and preparing, potential unevenness between sides or cases, and outcomes that depend more on the presiding judge's discipline.

In practice, many courts blend the two: fixed allotments as a default, with the presiding judge allowing extra time when the bench's questions run over.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: In appellate courts, the core tradeoff between strict fixed time limits and flexible judge-directed extensions pits docket predictability, focused advocacy, and formal parity against substantive depth and judicial candor. Strict limits force counsel to prioritize dispositive arguments, keep multi-case calendars running on schedule, and ensure visibly equal treatment between opposing sides. However, rigid clocks let strategic advocates evade difficult questions by running out the timer, while heavy bench questioning on a threshold issue can exhaust a party’s entire allotment before core merits arguments are heard. Conversely, judge-directed extensions allow panels to unpack complex records, test the downstream consequences of a proposed rule, and neutralize clock-management tactics, yielding better-informed deliberations. Yet flexibility carries real operational costs: daily calendars slip, later cases face fatigued judges, and asymmetrical extensions can give one side noticeably more airtime—risking perceptions of favoritism or unequal procedural footing, especially when repeat-player advocates draw longer exchanges. Ultimately, strict limits optimize institutional efficiency and symmetry, whereas flexible extensions prioritize decisional accuracy when briefing alone leaves hard questions unresolved.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The tradeoff is between predictability and fairness on one side, and depth of deliberation on the other.

Strict fixed limits, like the U.S. Supreme Court's traditional 30 minutes per side, which Chief Justice Rehnquist enforced almost to the second, keep the calendar on schedule and treat both parties equally. They also force lawyers to prioritize their strongest points. The downside is that a hot bench can use up a lawyer's time with questions, so key arguments may never be made. Judges with unresolved concerns may also have to rely only on the briefs or ask for supplemental filings.

Flexible extensions controlled by the judges let the court dig into hard or novel issues and finish a line of questioning. That can improve decision quality and give counsel a fuller hearing. The costs are an unpredictable docket and possible unequal treatment if one side gets more time. Lawyers also find it harder to plan, and the court's priorities can crowd out the advocate's.

Since 2020 the Supreme Court has shifted toward flexibility. Arguments now routinely run past the allotted time because of round-robin questioning, which shows the court accepting longer sessions in exchange for fuller exploration of the issues.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Strict fixed oral argument limits prioritize docket efficiency, schedule predictability, and formal parity between litigants. By holding each side to a hard allotment, courts keep crowded calendars moving and compel counsel to focus on decisive issues rather than repeating their briefs. The cost is rigidity: a hard cutoff can halt a clarifying exchange just as judges uncover a pivotal doctrinal or factual snag.

Flexible, judge-directed extensions invert that tradeoff. They allow the panel to pursue productive lines of questioning, test limiting principles, and probe complex or novel issues thoroughly. Yet flexibility brings practical friction. Unpredictable overruns cascade through the day's docket, straining court staff and waiting counsel. Extensions can also breed perceived unfairness when one side receives noticeably more time, even if driven by skeptical questioning, and can weaken the discipline that keeps advocacy concise. Most appellate courts balance these pressures by enforcing firm baseline limits while reserving brief, judge-initiated extensions strictly for active questioning rather than prepared speeches.
